newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Prospects grow for Swiss-Jewish compromise payment.
newsitem.headline: Prospects grow for Swiss-Jewish compromise payment.

text.p: Prospects for a compromise between Jewish groups and Switzerland have grown since Berne acknowledged it might compensate victims of the Nazis before an inquiry into its wartime role is over, officials said on Thursday.

Many Swiss say they still quietly share Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz's controversial view that Jewish calls for quickly establishing a Swiss memorial fund for Holocaust victims were tantamount to "blackmail".

But momentum for taking a fresh approach to neutral Switzerland's wartime record is boosting chances Berne will soon make a financial gesture demanded by Jewish groups who accuse Switzerland of cynically profitting from World War Two.

An elegant, face-saving solution put forward by Swiss Jews this week calls for repaying Jewish groups the 55 million Swiss francs ($40.49 million) they spent to support Jews who were allowed to enter Switzerland. No other refugees had to pay for their own upkeep.

Swiss shame at having turned back 30,000 refugees trying to escape Hitler -- most of them Jews -- still sits deep, and could be the key to unblocking a dispute that has prompted Jewish threats to call a boycott of Swiss banks.

Lili Nabholz, head of the lower house of parliament's legal affairs commission, said Berne had not decided yet on the issue, but the time was ripe for such a constructive proposal because taboos about questioning Switzerland's past were breaking down.

"There were always intellectuals and especially sensitised people who focused on this subject, but a broad public discussion on this theme is taking place for the first time," she said. "This is something new."

This also makes it harder for Swiss officials to maintain earlier insistence that any compensation payment had to await the result of a historians' commission just starting a broad review of whether the Swiss acted honourably during the war.
Jean-Francois Bergier, head of the international historians' panel appointed last month, said the Swiss were finally ready to take a more critical look at their own past.
"We were afraid of taking a ruthless look at history," he told Facts magazine in an interview. "Switzerland had always idealised its past and supressed aspects that did not fit."

Many prominent newspapers have come out in favour of making a financial gesture that goes beyond the government's plan to create a special fund by drawing on some 40 million Swiss francs in dormant bank accounts left over from the wartime era.

The weekly Weltwoche said Berne's wartime rejection of Jewish refugees and its ignominious plan to stamp their passports with "J" to make them easier to identify showed Switzerland still had a debt to pay to the Jewish community.

"The issue of guilt has long been settled. We made ourselves guilty," it wrote in a front-page commentary, adding: "Dealing honestly with our own history, where it shows dark spots, is not among our state virtues."
It dismissed talk that such a fund showed the Swiss were bowing to foreign pressure or displaying belated selflessness.

"Setting up a fund to benefit Holocaust survivors is not a generous gift to foreign beggars. It is a gesture of good will, an act of political decency and the compensation of injustice that has been committed," it said.
But the plan could still face opposition from conservatives in Berne backed by a vocal segment of the public.
"If the cabinet gives in now, more and more demands will follow," one letter to the mass-circulation Blick daily said, applauding Delamuraz for his "blackmail" comment.
"Minister Delamuraz only said what most Swiss think." ($1=1.3584 Swiss Franc)
